# Agents

A CLI tool that analyzes PHP code dependencies and visualizes the blast radius of changes. `peq <symbol>` draws what one symbol reaches, as a tree, for a person; `peq graph '<query>'` answers whatever can be written in GQL, as a table, for a program or an agent. Both write the same set of formats.

## Supported Versions

- **PHP peq runs on**: 8.3 / 8.4 / 8.5 — write source as a PHP 8.3 project: typed class
  constants, `readonly` classes, `#[\Override]`, and the rest of what 8.3 offers
- **PHP peq analyzes**: 5.6 – 8.5 with `native`, 7.1 – 8.5 with `phpstan` — the floor of
  each engine is the floor of what it is built on, and every version in range must keep
  working whichever runtime peq runs on

## Core Concepts

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 10 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  COMPOSER_NO_INTERACTION: '1'

jobs:
  tests:
    name: Tests on PHP ${{ matrix.php }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 25
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        php:
          - '8.3'
          - '8.4'
          - '8.5'
    steps:
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1

      - name: Set up PHP
        uses: shivammathur/setup-php@f3e473d116dcccaddc5834248c87452386958240
        with:
          php-version: ${{ matrix.php }}
          extensions: dom, filter, iconv, libxml, mbstring, pcntl, phar, simplexml, tokenizer, xmlwriter
          coverage: none
          ini-values: zend.assertions=1

      - name: Install dependencies
        uses: ramsey/composer-install@65e4f84970763564f46a70b8a54b90d033b3bdda
        with:
          dependency-versions: locked
          composer-options: --prefer-dist
          require-lock-file: 'true'

      - name: Check installed platform requirements
...

        run: composer deptrac

      - name: Keep ISO's artifacts between runs

どちらも手を打てます。Renovate の警告は、放置すると Actions の自動更新が止まったままになるので、先に直すのをおすすめします。Ubuntu 26 は今は壊れていないので、10/19 までに一度試しておけば十分です。

## 1. Renovate の警告

**原因:** `.github/workflows/release.yaml:22` のバージョンコメントが `# v4.0.0` になっていますが、`ramsey/composer-install` のタグには `v` が付かず、`4.0.0` です。Renovate は存在しないタグ `v4.0.0` を探して失敗しています。その結果、このActionは今後新しい版が出ても更新PRが来ません。

**調べる中で、もっと大きな問題が見つかりました。** 6つのワークフローのうち5つ(`ci.yaml`、`docs.yml`、`docs-preview.yml`、`equivalence.yml`、`pbt.yml`)は、Actionを SHA だけで指定していて、バージョンコメントがありません。Renovate は SHA だけではどの版か判断できないので、この5ファイルを更新対象にしていません。Dashboard でもこの5ファイルの依存は空になっています。実際、以前の Renovate PR #35(checkout を v7 に上げたもの)が変更したのは `release.yaml` だけでした。

- 今の状態: 全Actionの SHA を1つずつ確認したところ、どれも最新版を指していました。今すぐの実害はありません。
- 放置した場合: セキュリティ修正を含む新しい版が出ても、CI 側のワークフローには更新PRが来ません。

**対応:** PR を1本出します。`# 4.0.0` の修正と、5ファイルの SHA にバージョンコメント(`# v7.0.1` など)を付けるだけです。SHA は変えないので、CI の動きは何も変わりません。

5ファイルは php-ai-toolkit の導入時に生成されたものなので、toolkit のテンプレート自体がコメントなしで出力している可能性があります(未確認です)。そうだとすると、次に toolkit を適用したときに元に戻るので、toolkit 側も直す必要があるかもしれません。

## 2. Ubuntu 26 への移行

**何が起きるか:** 2026/10/19〜11/19 の間に、GitHub が `ubuntu-latest` の中身を 24.04 から 26.04 に順次切り替えます。peq のワークフローは6つとも `ubuntu-latest` なので、何もしなくても自動的に 26.04 で動くようになります。

**peq への影響は低いと見ています。**
- PHP は `setup-php` で入れていて、`setup-php` は `ubuntu-26.04` を公式にサポートしています。
- ワークフロー内に `apt` などの OS 固有のコマンドはありません。
- ただし、PHP 8.3/8.4 が 26.04 上で問題なく入るかは、実際に動かすまで分かりません。

**対応の選択肢:**
- **(おすすめ)事前に試す:** `runs-on` を `ubuntu-26.04` に変えた確認用のPRを出して CI を回し、結果を見たらマージせずに閉じます。通れば、それ以上することはありません。
- **何もしない:** 切り替え後に壊れたら直します。
- **`ubuntu-24.04` に固定する:** 問題を先送りするだけで、24.04 もいずれ廃止されるのでおすすめしません。

1 の修正PRと 2 の確認用PRを作ってよければ、進めます。どちらか片方だけでも対応できます。

## Why the renovate-approve app never approved anything

The [renovate-approve](https://github.com/apps/renovate-approve) app reacts to `pull_request.opened` (and `pull_request_review.dismissed`) and approves only when the pull request body contains `**Automerge**: Enabled` ([source](https://github.com/renovatebot/renovate-approve-bot/blob/main/index.js)). `renovate.json` never enabled automerge, so every Renovate pull request said `Automerge: Disabled by config` and the app skipped it.

Two more things kept "green CI → merge" from happening:

- Nothing enabled GitHub auto-merge on the Renovate pull requests (`autoMergeRequest` is `null` on all of them).
- The `main` branch protection requires a review but its required status check list is empty (`required_status_checks.checks: []`), so a merge does not wait for CI at all.

## What this pull request changes

- **`renovate.json`**: `automerge: true`, `automergeType: "pr"`, `platformAutomerge: true`. Renovate now writes `Automerge: Enabled` into each pull request, the app approves it when it opens, Renovate enables GitHub auto-merge on it (the repository already allows auto-merge), and GitHub merges it once the branch protection of `main` is satisfied.
- **`renovate.json`**: cap `phpunit/phpunit` below 11. PHPUnit 11 requires PHP 8.2, so the open v12 update (#37) fails `composer update` against the PHP 8.1 platform and can never turn green; Renovate closes it once this rule lands. The deprecated `matchPackagePatterns` is migrated to `matchPackageNames`.
- **`docs.yml` / `docs-preview.yml`**: previews of concurrent Renovate pull requests publish to the same `gh-pages` branch. A push rejected as non-fast-forward is now retried on the branch's current tip instead of failing the check that is about to become required.

Verification: `renovate-config-validator --strict` passes without migration hints, every `run:` script passes `bash -n`, and the retry loop was exercised locally against a simulated rejected push (shallow clone, another job publishing first): the second attempt landed and both previews were on the branch.

## Branch protection of `main` (needs repository admin; this pull request cannot change it)

Every job that runs on pull requests must be a required check, and branches must be up to date before merging:

```sh
gh api -X PATCH repos/k-kinzal/peq/branches/main/protection/required_status_checks --input - <<'EOF'
{
  "strict": true,
  "checks": [
    {"context": "Tests on PHP 8.1", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Tests on PHP 8.2", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Tests on PHP 8.3", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Tests on PHP 8.4", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Tests on PHP 8.5", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Lint", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Mutation testing", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Build the distributed binary", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Eris properties", "app_id": 15368},
    {"context": "Generate and publish the pull request preview", "app_id": 15368}
  ]
}
EOF
```

`app_id` 15368 is GitHub Actions, so only workflow runs can satisfy these contexts. `strict: true` makes GitHub wait until Renovate has rebased a pull request onto the current `main`, so CI always ran on what actually gets merged.

Keep the rest of the rule as follows:

- "Require a pull request before merging" with **1** approval. The app gives exactly one; install [renovate-approve-2](https://github.com/apps/renovate-approve-2) as well if two are required.
- "Require approval of the most recent reviewable push" must stay **off**. The app approves on open and after a dismissal, not after Renovate's rebases.
- "Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed" may stay on. The app re-approves when its own review is dismissed.
- Do not add `renovate/artifacts` as a required check unless `statusCheckWhen.artifactError` is set to `"always"`; by default the status is only reported on failure, so pull requests without artifact errors would wait for it forever.

## After merging

- The Renovate pull requests that are open now (#26, #30, #31, #32, #34, #35) were opened before this change, and the app only approves on `opened`. Approve them once by hand, or close them and tick their boxes on the Dependency Dashboard (#3) so Renovate recreates them. Renovate updates their body and enables auto-merge on its next run either way.
- With `strict: true` the queue drains one pull request at a time: after each merge Renovate rebases the others (`rebaseWhen=auto` resolves to `behind-base-branch` when automerge is on), re-enables auto-merge, CI reruns, and the next one merges.

## Decisions to review

- **Major updates are automerged too** when CI is green, as requested. CI never runs `release.yaml`, so a major bump of `softprops/action-gh-release` (#31) would merge on green without being exercised. To keep majors for a human, add this package rule:

  ```json
  {"matchUpdateTypes": ["major"], "automerge": false}
  ```

- The approve app is one way to satisfy the review requirement. The alternative is "Allow specified actors to bypass required pull requests" with the Renovate app as the actor; that works for rebases and pre-existing pull requests too and does not depend on webhook delivery.

--- Finish the toolkit adoption and fix the analyzer defects it exposed

Apply php-ai-toolkit the way the toolkit prescribes: one composer.lock
resolved for the PHP 8.1 platform floor, one phpunit.xml.dist, no test
runner script, workflows generated from the toolkit templates, and no
test helper layer — every test is a test method, a data provider or a
fixture next to the code it exercises. The PHPStan extensions the
configuration no longer includes are dropped from the dependencies.

Generated graphs are drawn from peq's own RandomSource instead of Faker:
Faker's generator reseeded mt_rand from its destructor, so the graph a
seed produced depended on garbage collection.

Working through the mutation gate exposed defects in the analyzer:

- PHPStan strips the bodies of functions in files its parser has not
  been told are analysed, so a free function's body never reached the
  collectors and produced no relations. The analyzer now registers the
  analysed files with the parser, as PHPStan's own commands do.
- A file PHPStan could not finish was silently left out of the graph,
  which read as "nothing depends on it". Such a failure is now an
  AnalysisFailedException.
- The scratch directory PHPStan was configured from was removed right
  after the container was built, so PHPStan rebuilt it under every
  analysis to write its cache — one directory left behind per analysis
  — and compiled a new container class per analysis, which a test suite
  paid for in memory and time. PHPStan now works in one directory per
  user, with the configuration named after its contents.
- A recoverable syntax error made the reparsed source report a partial
  tree as if it were the file; it now reports nothing for that file.

The declaration collector hands every parameter to the promoted-property
processor, which decides what promotes a property, and no longer lists
the `$this`-bound usages that cannot occur outside a method body. The
file collector's directory exclusion was a strict subset of its path
exclusion and is gone.

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M2S89SCV14T92VKQWXJ5J74R

--- Fix CI: enable assertions at startup and record generated graphs portably

The CI runners' production php.ini starts PHP with zend.assertions=-1,
which PHPUnit's <ini> cannot raise at runtime; failOnAllIssues turned
that warning into a failure in every job that runs PHPUnit. The test,
mutation and property jobs now start PHP with zend.assertions=1.

The recorded graphs for a seed failed on PHP 8.1 and 8.2 because Faker
seeds PHP's Mersenne Twister in its legacy mode below 8.3. The
generators only ever draw a number, a boolean and a word, so they now
depend on a RandomSource contract instead of Faker's magic-method
Generator. peq keeps drawing from Faker through FakerRandomSource, and
the record is taken from PortableDraws, a xorshift source whose sequence
is the same on every runtime.

## Actions Best Practices

Apply these rules to every workflow created by this skill:

- Pin every external action with the full 40-character commit SHA.
- Keep workflow YAML free of explanatory comments, including release-tag comments
  after action SHAs. Use clear job and step names.
- Verify each SHA from the action's original repository:
  ```bash
  gh release view --repo actions/checkout --json tagName,publishedAt,url
  git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/actions/checkout.git 'refs/tags/<tag>'
  ```
- Use top-level `permissions: contents: read` and only grant additional
  permissions for a step that truly needs them.
- Use `pull_request`, not `pull_request_target`, for untrusted PR code.
- Use `concurrency` with PR number or ref and `cancel-in-progress: true`.
  Include the event name so a manual whole-tree mutation run cannot cancel the PR
  checks on the same branch.
- Set `fail-fast: false` for version matrices so all supported minors report.
- Add `timeout-minutes` to jobs.
- Give every job and every step a clear `name`.
- Do not use `continue-on-error` for required lint or test gates.
- When versioned lock files are used, copy the matching lock to `composer.lock`
  before validation and installation, then install with locked dependencies and
  `require-lock-file: true`. Run `composer check-platform-reqs` after installation.
- When no lock file is committed, do not claim `dependency-versions: locked` and
  do not set `require-lock-file: true`; deliberately install the dependency mode
  the project chose.
- Let `ramsey/composer-install` handle Composer caching; do not add a second
  Composer cache step unless the project has a measured reason.

Job timeouts, PHP memory limits, and worker counts are operational starting
points. Measure sustained runtime, peak memory, and runner capacity, then adjust
them with headroom. Never use those settings to narrow a gate, skip targets, or
turn a quality failure into a pass. The template's values are not target-project
facts.
